## My Thinking

I have about 10 mu of land my family has worked for years. In Quzhou, everyone grows winter wheat and summer maize — that is the rotation. It is what my father did, what my neighbors do, and what the grain stations buy. I am not going to try cotton or vegetables. The market is unpredictable and I do not have the connections to sell specialty crops.

My wheat was already sown last October and is jointing right now. I need to irrigate it once more before heading, spray for powdery mildew, and top-dress nitrogen. After harvest in June I will plant maize immediately on the same land — no gap, that is how we maximize the season.

For seeds, the township agricultural station subsidizes improved wheat varieties (石麦 or 衡麦 type). I will use those — the subsidy makes it cheap and the yield is reliable. For maize I always buy hybrid seed from the supply cooperative,郑单958 or similar. Hybrid is standard now, everyone uses it.

I apply fertilizer by habit and by what the seed bag says. I probably use a bit more urea than strictly needed — I would rather not under-fertilize and lose yield than save a few yuan on nitrogen. Same with irrigation: Quzhou is dry, groundwater is what we have, and I will not risk the crop wilting at heading time. I pump four times for wheat and two times for maize if summer rain is short.

For tillage, I switched to rotary tillage a few years ago. Saves diesel and time. The combine leaves straw and the rotary tiller chops it in. I do not plough deep anymore.

Immediately after the combine finishes in June I direct-seed hybrid maize into the stubble with no-tillage to keep moisture and save time, relying mainly on summer rainfall but pumping once or twice if August turns dry. I use subsidy-supported improved wheat varieties and cooperative-supplied hybrid maize seed, apply fertilizer at rates I know from experience, and irrigate conservatively to protect yield rather than save water, because groundwater is available and losing a harvest would hurt the family badly.
